flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: The text says otherwise. Jacob wakes and “…he was afraid…” (Gen 28:17) Then he says, “How awesome is this place!” (Gen 28:17) Afraid is the word the text uses, so I think calm isn't the right picture, baker.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Right, and here's what the text says. “…he was afraid…” (Gen 28:17) Jacob had just said, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.” (Gen 28:16) So he's afraid, not calm, and he calls the place awesome.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.answerText: Food to eat and clothes to wear
flags.explanation: Jacob's vow goes on, “…if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear…” (Gen 28:20) That's another IF in the vow, baker. The list is food and clothes. Simple things.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Half is a lot bigger than what he says. Jacob says, “…of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.” (Gen 28:22) A tenth is the amount in the verse, baker. Not half.

flags.problem: “Same stone, new job” makes a joke about the pillar Jacob identifies as God’s house (Genesis 28:22). Holy things are not to be the joke.
flags.answerText: Sets it up as a pillar and pours oil on it
flags.explanation: The text says, “…Jacob took the stone that he had placed under his head, and he set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it…” (Gen 28:18) The stone he slept on becomes the pillar. Same stone, new job, baker. He does this early the next morning.

flags.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
flags.explanation: That's right, baker, they're bells. Verse 25 says, "They also made bells of pure gold and attached them around the hem between the pomegranates…" (Exodus 39:25) Verse 26 says the bells and pomegranates alternate around the lower hem. So it goes bell, pomegranate, bell, pomegranate, all the way around.

flags.problem: This repeats the word memorial without explaining it or adding much of Papa Dorin's personality.
flags.explanation: Yes, the word is memorial, baker. Verse 7 says they fastened the stones on the shoulder pieces "…as memorial stones for the sons of Israel…" (Exodus 39:7) That's the word the text gives. They did it as the LORD had commanded Moses.

flags.problem: The explanation repeats the answer several times, and its last sentence adds no explanation or personality.
flags.explanation: Boundary stones are a real thing, but this verse uses a different word. Exodus 39:7 says these were "…memorial stones for the sons of Israel…" So the word that fits is memorial. Same stones, and the text picks memorial.

flags.problem: The explanation restates the engraving three times without adding a distinct Papa Dorin touch.
flags.explanation: There's no line from the law on these stones. Verse 14 says each of the twelve stones was "…engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes." (Exodus 39:14) So each stone carries a tribe's name. That's what the verse says is engraved.

flags.problem: The last two sentences repeat the verse's reason rather than developing the explanation or sounding like Papa Dorin.
flags.answerText: So it sits higher on the neck
flags.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about height, friend. Exodus 39:23 says the collar was around the opening "…so that it would not tear." That's the reason it gives. The collar is there to keep the opening from tearing.

flags.problem: The explanation is generic and repeats the same reason in its last two sentences.
flags.answerText: So it can be tied shut
flags.explanation: Nothing in the verse mentions tying. Exodus 39:23 says the collar was around the opening "…so that it would not tear." That's the reason the text gives. So the collar is there to keep the opening from tearing.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through the verse but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Servant is a good word, but it isn't what's engraved. Exodus 39:30 says the inscription reads "HOLY TO THE LORD." Those are the words on the plate of the holy crown. The verse says that plate is pure gold.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of the verse but has no closing ellipsis.
flags.explanation: It's actually true, baker. Right after the holy crown, verse 32 says, "So all the work for the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting, was completed." (Exodus 39:32) The same verse says the Israelites did everything just as the LORD had commanded Moses. So the work is complete.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through the verse but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.answerText: He gives them a day off
flags.explanation: A day off sounds nice, friend, but the text doesn't say that. Exodus 39:43 says Moses inspected the work and saw they had done it just as the LORD had commanded. Then it says, "So Moses blessed them." That's what he does.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through the verse but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: A feast would be fun, and I'd bring cookies, but the verse doesn't say that. Exodus 39:43 says Moses saw they had done it just as the LORD had commanded. Then it says, "So Moses blessed them." A blessing is what the text gives.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.answerText: See the land given to Israel
flags.explanation: That's the job, friend. The LORD says, "Go up this mountain of the Abarim range and see the land that I have given the Israelites." (Numbers 27:12) Notice the word "given." The LORD calls it land He has given to the Israelites, and Moses gets to look at it from up there.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.answerText: A man to lead the congregation
flags.explanation: That's it. Moses asks the LORD to "…appoint a man over the congregation…" (Numbers 27:16) He asks this right after hearing he'll be gathered to his people. I think his request shows how much he cares about who leads them next.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Yes, sheep. Moses says he doesn't want the congregation of the LORD to be "…like sheep without a shepherd." (Numbers 27:17) It's a picture of people with no one to lead them. Matthew 9:36 describes the crowds with the same words, "…like sheep without a shepherd."

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Right, False. Nothing happens in a back room here. God tells Moses, "Have him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, and commission him in their sight." (Numbers 27:19) That's out in the open, with the whole congregation there to see it.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: True. The text says, "Moses did as the LORD had commanded him." (Numbers 27:22) Then it tells what he did: he took Joshua and had him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation. He had just heard God say he'd be gathered to his people, so I think that's a lot to take in and still do.

flags.problem: The claim that Moses walked with the people all that way is a Bible-history assertion without a reference.
flags.explanation: Ooh, I know why this one sounds right. A leader walks his people all that way, so you expect him to walk in with them. But God doesn't say that. He says, "After you have seen it, you too will be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron was…" (Numbers 27:13) Seeing the land comes first, then Moses is gathered to his people. I think that's a heavy thing to hear.

flags.problem: The quotation from Matthew 9:36 has no reference.
flags.explanation: Yes, sheep. Moses says he doesn't want the congregation of the LORD to be "…like sheep without a shepherd." (Numbers 27:17) It's a picture of people with no one to lead them. Matthew 9:36 describes the crowds with the same words, "…like sheep without a shepherd."

flags.problem: The explanation repeats that God named the Spirit without adding insight or sounding distinctly like Papa Dorin.
flags.explanation: Spirit is right. God calls Joshua "…a man with the Spirit in him…" (Numbers 27:18) That's the description God gives when He tells Moses to take Joshua son of Nun. Out of everything God could point to, it's the Spirit.

flags.problem: This explanation closely repeats the structure and wording of the explanation for mercy, rather than sounding different from it.
flags.explanation: Blessing is a nice thought, but it's not the word in this verse. God says Eleazar "…will seek counsel for him before the LORD by the judgment of the Urim." (Numbers 27:21) The word is counsel. Eleazar the priest seeks it for Joshua.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Correct, baker. The text says "…the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem." It's a little hard to read after that long list of cities, but the writer tells it straight. That's the one spot where Judah couldn't drive them out, and the verse says so plainly (Joshua 15:63).

flags.problem: The text does not say that every dry spot in the Negev needs springs.
flags.explanation: True, baker! Acsah asks for springs, and the verse says "…Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs." She asked her dad for water, and he gave her both sets. I love that for her. Every dry spot in the Negev needs a spring or two (Joshua 15:19).

flags.problem: Calling Jerusalem the one spot where Judah could not drive people out goes beyond the text. The passage does not say it was the only such place.
flags.explanation: Correct, baker. The text says "…the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem." It's a little hard to read after that long list of cities, but the writer tells it straight. That's the one spot where Judah couldn't drive them out, and the verse says so plainly (Joshua 15:63).

flags.problem: The sandals line is mild rather than a clear laugh, where the size of Saul's search party leaves room for one.
flags.explanation: Three thousand it is. Saul takes "…three thousand chosen men from all Israel…" and goes looking for David and his men (1 Samuel 24:2). That's a LOT of sandals on one dusty road.

flags.problem: It says David's action surprises everybody, but the text does not describe their reaction.
flags.explanation: Enemy is right. David's men say, "This is the day about which the LORD said to you, ’Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do with him as you wish.’…" (1 Samuel 24:4). They say it with Saul in the cave. Then David creeps up, and what he does next surprises everybody.

flags.problem: The opening mark on the nested quotation is incorrect, and the ellipsis is added after the completed quotation.
flags.explanation: Enemy is right. David's men say, "This is the day about which the LORD said to you, ’Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do with him as you wish.’…" (1 Samuel 24:4). They say it with Saul in the cave. Then David creeps up, and what he does next surprises everybody.

flags.problem: The statement about what David's men had said needs a reference to 1 Samuel 24:4; the reference to verse 7 does not cover it.
flags.explanation: True. "With these words David restrained his men, and he did not let them rise up against Saul." (1 Samuel 24:7). Those men had just said this was the day the LORD spoke of. David answered them with words, and the men did not rise up.

flags.problem: The text says Saul looked behind him and David bowed; it does not say Saul saw him in the dirt.
flags.explanation: David calls out, "My lord the king!" and then "…David bowed facedown in reverence…" (1 Samuel 24:8). Saul looks behind him and sees a man on his face in the dirt. I think a bow like that shows David's respect for Saul.

flags.problem: The nested quotation starts with a closing single quotation mark instead of the BSB's opening single quotation mark.
flags.explanation: Harm is right. David asks, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ’Look, David intends to harm you’?" (1 Samuel 24:9). I think he's asking Saul to think about who he's listening to. Then he points Saul to what happened in the cave.

flags.problem: The nested quotation starts with a closing single quotation mark instead of the BSB's opening single quotation mark.
flags.explanation: Mock isn't the word. David asks, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ’Look, David intends to harm you’?" (1 Samuel 24:9). The men David mentions say he means to harm the king. That's the word that fills the blank.

flags.problem: The explanation mechanically repeats the answer without adding much beyond the quoted verse.
flags.explanation: Mock isn't the word. David asks, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ’Look, David intends to harm you’?" (1 Samuel 24:9). The men David mentions say he means to harm the king. That's the word that fills the blank.

flags.problem: It states that a dead dog is small, which the text does not say and is not necessarily true.
flags.explanation: Those are big, scary animals, and David doesn't use them here. He asks, "Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea?" (1 Samuel 24:14). I think he's showing Saul how little there is to chase. A dead dog and a flea are small and low, nothing like a lion or a bear.

flags.problem: It calls David's words a prayer and says the king is standing right there. The text presents David speaking to Saul and does not specify their distance or Saul's posture.
flags.explanation: Saul's hand. David prays, "May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15). He's speaking to Saul while he asks the LORD to plead his case. I think that's a bold way to pray with the king standing right there.

flags.problem: The partial quotation "my father" needs ellipses to show where it cuts into the verse.
flags.explanation: Servant isn't what Saul says. He calls out, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). David had called him "my father" (1 Samuel 24:11), and Saul answers with a family word too. The word is son.

flags.problem: The partial quotation "my father" needs ellipses to show where it cuts into the verse.
flags.explanation: Friend is a nice word, but Saul uses another. He calls out, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). David had called him "my father" (1 Samuel 24:11), so Saul answers in the same family way. Then Saul weeps aloud.

flags.problem: Saul says the kingdom will be established in David's hands; he does not say establishing it is the work of a king.
flags.explanation: Priest isn't the word. Saul says, "Now I know for sure that you will be king…" (1 Samuel 24:20). He goes on to say that "…the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands." (1 Samuel 24:20). That's the work of a king.

flags.problem: It says David goes the other way, but the text gives their destinations, not their relative directions.
flags.explanation: Keilah isn't named here. The text says "…David and his men went up to the stronghold." (1 Samuel 24:22). Saul heads home, and David goes the other way, up to the stronghold. They split up.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.answerText: The LORD found some good in him
flags.explanation: Ahijah tells her in verse 13 that this boy is the only one belonging to Jeroboam who will receive a proper burial, "…because only in him has the LORD, the God of Israel, found any good in the house of Jeroboam." Out of a whole house, one boy is singled out. I think that's a quiet kindness tucked inside a hard message.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: True. In verse 14 Ahijah says the LORD "…will raise up for Himself a king over Israel who will cut off the house of Jeroboam." The king is raised up for the LORD Himself. That matches verse 10, where the house of Jeroboam was already named in the disaster.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: In verse 15 Ahijah says the LORD will uproot Israel "…from this good land that He gave their fathers…" The land was a gift to those who came before them. To be uprooted from a gift is a heavy thing, I think.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Ahijah says in verse 16 that God will give Israel over "…on account of the sins Jeroboam has committed and has caused Israel to commit." That's two things: what Jeroboam did and what he led Israel into. Verse 15 names the Asherah poles Israel made, provoking the LORD to anger.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: True. Verse 17 says, "…as soon as she stepped over the threshold of the house, the boy died." Ahijah had told her the child would die when her feet entered the city (1 Kings 14:12). It's a heavy moment, friend.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Verse 20 says, "…his son Nadab reigned in his place." Jeroboam's reign lasted twenty-two years, and then he rested with his fathers. After that the throne goes to Nadab.

flags.problem: “Heart first, friend, always” sounds like a preachy slogan rather than a natural explanation of the verse.
flags.answerText: Followed God with all his heart
flags.explanation: In verse 8 God speaks through Ahijah, and He says David "…kept My commandments and followed Me with all his heart, doing only what was right in My eyes." That's the measure God holds up. It's about David's heart following Him. Heart first, friend, always.

flags.problem: The opening jokes about how many lines prophets get in the chapter. The way Scripture is written is never the joke.
flags.explanation: Prophets get lots of lines in this chapter, since one is doing the talking. But in verse 15 Ahijah says the land is the one "…that He gave their fathers…" The word there is fathers, not prophets. The land came to them first, and the message is about Israel being uprooted from it.

flags.problem: Solomon is introduced only as a name from earlier in the story, not as a person. The explanation should briefly identify him without relying on an earlier passage.
flags.explanation: Solomon is a name from earlier in the story, and he's gone by now. 1 Kings 11:43 says he rested with his fathers and Rehoboam reigned in his place. Ahijah's words in verse 16 are about "…the sins Jeroboam has committed and has caused Israel to commit."

flags.problem: Asking an oven for advice is not a relatable comparison to David seeking direction. An oven cannot answer him.
flags.answerText: He asks God what to do
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. David inquired of God: "Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?" (1 Chronicles 14:10). He brought the question straight to God instead of guessing. I wish I'd asked my oven before I tried a batch with it turned off.

flags.problem: This closely repeats the first explanation's structure, quotations, and phrase about a clear yes and a promise. Explanations should sound different from one another.
flags.explanation: Actually it's true, friend. David asked, "Will You deliver them into my hand?" and the LORD replied, "Go," and then "for I will deliver them into your hand." (1 Chronicles 14:10). He got a clear yes and a promise, no maybe about it.

flags.problem: “Hold on to the gods” is confusing. It can sound like advice to cling to the Philistines' gods rather than remember the answer.
flags.explanation: Not the king, baker. The verse says the Philistines "…abandoned their gods…" at Baal-perazim (1 Chronicles 14:12). That's the thing the text says they left. It names no king there, so hold on to the gods.

flags.problem: The joke about three cities being in the running turns the answer choices into a contest. Papa Dorin does not joke about the lesson's questions.
flags.explanation: Nineveh is a famous address, baker, but it's not on this scroll's mailing label. The scroll is found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media (Ezra 6:2). The search itself was ordered for the archives stored in the treasury of Babylon (Ezra 6:1). Three cities were in the running, and Ecbatana takes the prize.

flags.problem: “Not quite, baker” is a reaction. The explanation must not include one.
flags.explanation: Not quite, baker. The memo says, "The costs are to be paid from the royal treasury." (Ezra 6:4). So the building costs come from the royal treasury, not from the Jews. The size is in the memo too, sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide (Ezra 6:3). Plans and a payment source, all in one memo.

flags.problem: The explanation repeats the same point and ends with “That's a true statement.” It feels flat and generic rather than like Papa Dorin.
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says Tattenai, Shethar-bozenai and their associates "…diligently carried out what King Darius had decreed." (Ezra 6:13). Diligently is the word the text gives. They did what the king decreed. That's a true statement.

flags.problem: “Wrong building site” uses “wrong” about the baker's answer, which Papa Dorin must not do.
flags.explanation: Elijah and Elisha are famous, baker, but they're not named in this verse. The text says the elders built and prospered "…through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo." (Ezra 6:14). Those are the two prophets for this building. Right fame, wrong building site.

flags.problem: “Wrong crew” uses “wrong” about the baker's answer, which Papa Dorin must not do.
flags.explanation: Haggai and Zechariah are the prophets in this passage, friend, and they come in with the building (Ezra 6:14). But the text gives the slaughtering to others: "…the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their priestly brothers, and for themselves." (Ezra 6:20). So it's the Levites, not the prophets. Right passage, wrong crew.

flags.problem: It has 6 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.answerText: God has chosen a new king
flags.explanation: A new king, friend? Whoa, whoa, whoa. That's a whole different headline, and this psalm never prints it. What the many say is, "God will not deliver him." (Psalm 3:2). That's about whether God will rescue David, and nothing else. Don't let your brain bake in an extra ingredient the recipe never called for.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: True. David says the LORD is "…my glory, and the One who lifts my head." (Psalm 3:3). Verse 2 has many saying, "God will not deliver him." and verse 3 begins with "But You, O LORD…" I think a lifted head is a mighty fine thing to have when the crowd is that loud.

flags.problem: The psalm says enemies are set against David on every side, not that they are closing in on him.
flags.explanation: A river, friend? I can see it now: David standing there with enemies closing in, and the LORD is a nice, relaxing stream. Lovely for a picnic, not so much for a battle. David says, "But You, O LORD, are a shield around me…" (Psalm 3:3). A shield is what he reaches for, and it goes all the way around him.

flags.problem: The joke imagines the LORD as a relaxing stream and makes that image the punchline. Papa Dorin's humor must not target God.
flags.explanation: A river, friend? I can see it now: David standing there with enemies closing in, and the LORD is a nice, relaxing stream. Lovely for a picnic, not so much for a battle. David says, "But You, O LORD, are a shield around me…" (Psalm 3:3). A shield is what he reaches for, and it goes all the way around him.

flags.problem: The sense-of-direction line is a familiar, mild joke. It reads more like a pleasant dad than Papa Dorin's funny, self-deprecating voice.
flags.explanation: That's it, friend. The verse says "…for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." (Psalm 67:4). So the nations get a Judge and a Leader. I'd follow that guide way before I'd follow my own sense of direction.

flags.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
flags.answerText: So the righteous won't turn to injustice
flags.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says the scepter of the wicked will not rest on the land, "…so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice." (Psalm 125:3) That's the reason the psalm gives. The scepter is the wicked ruler's staff of power. The psalm says it won't settle on the land given to the righteous.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. The psalm says, "But those who turn to crooked ways the LORD will banish with the evildoers." (Psalm 125:5) I think this is a heavy line. It comes right after the prayer, "Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to the upright in heart." (Psalm 125:4)

flags.problem: The cookie comparison does not fit: a tray disappearing as someone walks past suggests a very short time, not a season. The joke fails the logic test.
flags.explanation: Careful, friend, this one's flipped. The psalm says the opposite: Mount Zion "…cannot be moved; it abides forever." (Psalm 125:1) A season is about how long a fresh tray of my cookies lasts once somebody walks past the counter. Forever is a whole other category. The psalm says the people who trust the LORD are like that mountain.

flags.problem: “I like your heart on that one” assumes the baker’s motive or attitude from the answer they picked. Papa Dorin has not been told that.
flags.answerText: So the wicked will turn and repent
flags.explanation: I like your heart on that one, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. The reason it gives is "…so that the righteous will not put forth their hands to injustice." (Psalm 125:3) The verse says nothing about the wicked turning around. Its reason is about the righteous.

flags.problem: The kitchen-light comparison merely restates the image and has no punchline, despite room for a laugh.
flags.explanation: Light it is, friend. The Teacher says "…wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness…" (Ecclesiastes 2:13). He looks at wisdom and folly side by side and gives wisdom the win. It's like flipping on the kitchen light and finally seeing where the cookie sheet actually is.

flags.problem: The explanation repeats that the mind does not rest without adding much personality or insight.
flags.explanation: Mind it is, baker. The Teacher says, "even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Even at night, the mind keeps going. The verse names the mind as what does not rest.

flags.problem: The explanation is flat and repetitive. The opening about tired hands sets up an opportunity for a relatable laugh but does not deliver one.
flags.explanation: You'd think tired hands would finally get a rest, friend. But the verse says, "even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Hands aren't mentioned there. It's the mind that does not rest.

flags.problem: The explanation is generic and repeats the distinction between the mind and the household without bringing Papa Dorin's voice to it.
flags.explanation: His household isn't mentioned in this verse, baker. The Teacher says, "even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). The trouble named is his mind. It isn't the people around him.

flags.problem: The explanation simply repeats the answer and rules out gathering. It misses an opportunity for Papa Dorin's humor or a more distinctive observation.
flags.answerText: To gather more than anyone before him
flags.explanation: Gathering isn't what he calls better, baker. He says, "Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work." (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Piling up more isn't part of that. Enjoying the work is.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through the verse but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: I see why you'd think it, but it's the opposite. Isaiah says of them, "They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD." (Isaiah 31:1). They're looking at the horses and not at Him. It's like telling a friend you're listening while your eyes never leave your phone.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through the verse but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: False, and Isaiah says it plainly: "They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD." (Isaiah 31:1). Their trust sits in the horses, the chariots and the horsemen. The LORD isn't on that list, and the woe is aimed at exactly these people.

flags.problem: The quotation omits words both before and after it in the verse without ellipses.
flags.answerText: He does not call them back
flags.explanation: Yes! Isaiah says of the LORD, "He does not call back His words." (Isaiah 31:2). Once He has spoken, it stands. I can't say that about myself. I've called back "I'm only having one cookie" more times than I can count.

flags.problem: The quotation omits words both before and after it in the verse without ellipses.
flags.explanation: Not quite. Isaiah says the opposite: "He does not call back His words." (Isaiah 31:2). Nothing in the verse has Him swapping them out later. His words stand, and that includes the part about disaster.

flags.problem: The quotation omits words both before and after it in the verse without ellipses.
flags.explanation: Close, but no. Isaiah doesn't mention hiding anything. He says, "He does not call back His words." (Isaiah 31:2). The point is that He doesn't take them back. What He has said stays said.

flags.problem: The second quotation stops before the end of the verse without an ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Both, baker. Isaiah says "…the helper will stumble, and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together." (Isaiah 31:3). I think this one is heavy, so I'll say it plainly. The helper doesn't stand off to the side while the other one falls. Just before this, Isaiah says "…the Egyptians are men, not God; their horses are flesh, not spirit." (Isaiah 31:3).

flags.problem: Papa jokes about what he would do in the lion's place, but the lion is the comparison for the LORD in this verse.
flags.explanation: True! The LORD says the lion "…is not terrified by their shouting or subdued by their clamor…" (Isaiah 31:4). A whole band of shepherds is called out against it, making all that noise, and it isn't scared. I'd have been halfway to the next county. My mustache would've been a white flag.

flags.problem: The first quotation stops before the end of the verse without an ellipsis. The second starts partway through the verse without an opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: I get it, after all that woe it might feel that way. But the verse says, "Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem." (Isaiah 31:5). It goes right on to say, "He will shield it and deliver it…" (Isaiah 31:5). Those are words of protecting, not abandoning.

flags.problem: The first quotation stops before the end of the verse without an ellipsis. The second starts partway through the verse without an opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Not this time. The verse says, "Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem." It goes on, "He will shield it and deliver it…" (Isaiah 31:5). Nothing in this picture is a test. The word is protect.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of the verse without an ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Right, baker! The LORD says Assyria will fall "…not by the sword of man; a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals." (Isaiah 31:8). So this is a sword that mortals did not make. I think this verse is a heavy one, so I'll just say it plainly. The answer is what the LORD said: not made by mortals.

flags.problem: The first quotation omits words both before and after it in the verse without ellipses.
flags.explanation: Egypt comes up earlier in this passage, but not here. The LORD says, "a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals." (Isaiah 31:8). Since mortals didn't make that sword, a forge in Egypt isn't the answer. Assyria falls "…not by the sword of man…" (Isaiah 31:8).

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of the verse without an ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Good thinking, but the verse doesn't point to anyone's army. The LORD says Assyria will fall "…not by the sword of man; a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals." (Isaiah 31:8). Judah's army isn't named in the verse. The answer has to match what the verse says about the sword.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through the verse but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Not this time. The LORD says, "They will flee before the sword, and their young men will be put to forced labor." (Isaiah 31:8). Assyria flees instead of holding its ground. That's the opposite of standing and fighting it out.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through the verse but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: False, baker. The LORD says, "They will flee before the sword, and their young men will be put to forced labor." (Isaiah 31:8). They flee, so they don't stand their ground. I think this verse is a heavy one, with the forced labor in it.

flags.problem: The quotation uses a closing single quotation mark before Obey instead of the BSB’s opening single quotation mark.
flags.explanation: Once? Oh no, no, no, friend. God says, "…I strongly warned them again and again, saying, ’Obey My voice.’…" (Jeremiah 11:7). Again and again is a long way from one time. That's a whole lot of warning from Egypt until that day.

flags.problem: The quotation uses a closing single quotation mark before Obey instead of the BSB’s opening single quotation mark.
flags.explanation: False is right, friend. God says, "…I strongly warned them again and again, saying, ’Obey My voice.’…" (Jeremiah 11:7). That's far more than once. The warnings stretched from the time of Egypt until that day.

flags.problem: Saying the word was hard for Jeremiah to carry attributes difficulty to him without marking it as Papa Dorin’s thought.
flags.explanation: Not this time, friend. God tells Jeremiah, "…do not pray for these people." (Jeremiah 11:14). He even adds that Jeremiah shouldn't raise up a cry or a prayer on their behalf. This one is a hard word for Jeremiah to carry.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Yes, light. The man says, "He has driven me away and made me walk in darkness instead of light." (Lamentations 3:2) Notice he says he's walking in the darkness, friend. I think this is a man who's tired of not being able to see where he's going.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: True. He says, "He pierced my kidneys with His arrows." (Lamentations 3:13) It comes right after the bow and the target in verse 12. I think this one hurts, friend, and it's okay to say so.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: A prophet is a natural guess, friend, but it's not the word the king uses. In Daniel 3:28 Nebuchadnezzar says God "…has sent His angel and delivered His servants who trusted in Him." Angel is the word in his declaration.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: A priest isn't who the king names, friend. In Daniel 3:28 Nebuchadnezzar says God "…has sent His angel and delivered His servants who trusted in Him." The word he uses is angel.

flags.problem: The quotation uses “I,” but the explanation does not name Nebuchadnezzar as the speaker before quoting him.
flags.answerText: Another chance to bow when the music plays
flags.explanation: That's right, baker. Daniel 3:15 says that when they hear the music, "…if you are ready to fall down and worship the statue I have made, very good." Then he adds that if they refuse, they will be thrown at once into the blazing fiery furnace. So he gives them another chance first, and the warning comes after.

flags.problem: The treasure-map and shovel joke does not match the action in the verse: amassing what is not his and making himself rich with loans.
flags.explanation: No treasure map here, baker. The taunt says, "Woe to him who amasses what is not his and makes himself rich with many loans!" (Habakkuk 2:6). The verse names loans and never mentions hidden treasure. Hidden treasure is a fun guess, though, and I'd have grabbed a shovel too.

flags.problem: It says the creditors both arise and awaken. The verse says the creditors arise and those who disturb him awaken, without explicitly identifying the two groups as the same.
flags.explanation: Oh, I wish it worked that way, friend, but it doesn't. The verse asks, "Will not your creditors suddenly arise and those who disturb you awaken? Then you will become their prey." (Habakkuk 2:7). Forgetting isn't in there. The creditors arise and awaken.

flags.problem: The woe is directed at the man who builds his house by unjust gain, not at the gain itself.
flags.explanation: That's the word, baker. "Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain…" (Habakkuk 2:9). This is the second woe. The woe falls on the unjust gain behind the house.

flags.problem: “We've all felt safer” assumes an experience and feeling the baker has not shared.
flags.explanation: You got it, friend. The verse says, "Woe to him who builds his house by unjust gain, to place his nest on high and escape the hand of disaster!" (Habakkuk 2:9). I think he figured a nest up high would keep disaster from reaching him. We've all felt safer just by getting farther from the problem.

flags.problem: The final sentence states a fact from Habakkuk 2:15 without giving that verse's reference.
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. The verse says, "You will be filled with shame instead of glory." (Habakkuk 2:16). Shame takes the place of glory. It comes in the woe for the one who gives his neighbors drink until they are drunk.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through a sentence but does not show an ellipsis where it cuts in.
flags.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about breaking, friend. It says, "he makes idols that cannot speak." (Habakkuk 2:18). Speaking is the problem here. The idol can't say a word.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through a sentence but does not show an ellipsis where it cuts in.
flags.explanation: Cost isn't the point here, baker. The verse says, "he makes idols that cannot speak." (Habakkuk 2:18). The maker trusts his own creation, and it can't say a word.

flags.problem: The sprinkles comparison does not match the action in the verse. A cookie is not something that is presented as having breath, so the joke does not click.
flags.explanation: Right, baker. The verse says, "Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, yet there is no breath in it at all." (Habakkuk 2:19). Sprinkles on a cookie don't make it breathe, and gold doesn't either. The shine is on the outside, and there's no breath in it.

flags.problem: The quotation beginning “let all the earth” cuts into the sentence without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: That's right, friend. The verse says, "let all the earth be silent before Him." (Habakkuk 2:20). It comes right after "…the LORD is in His holy temple…" All the earth is called to be silent before Him.

flags.problem: The quotation beginning “let all the earth” cuts into the sentence without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: I love a good shout, baker, and you know I'm loud. But the verse says, "let all the earth be silent before Him." (Habakkuk 2:20). Silence is what's asked here.

flags.problem: The quotation beginning “let all the earth” cuts into the sentence without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Gifts aren't mentioned, friend. The verse says, "let all the earth be silent before Him." (Habakkuk 2:20). Quiet is the whole request.

flags.problem: The two sentences after the quote repeat that Herod named John without adding much. The explanation feels flat.
flags.answerText: John the Baptist risen from the dead
flags.explanation: Matthew says Herod heard the reports about Jesus (Matthew 14:1), and then Herod tells his servants, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him." (Matthew 14:2). Herod puts a name on it, and the name is John. He says it out loud to his servants, no hedging.

flags.problem: Herod's quoted speech stops before he finishes speaking, but the quote has no ellipsis at the end.
flags.explanation: Elijah is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the name Herod says. Matthew records Herod telling his servants, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!" (Matthew 14:2). Herod puts the miraculous powers down to John. Elijah never comes up in his words.

flags.problem: Herod's quoted speech stops before he finishes speaking, but the quote has no ellipsis at the end.
flags.explanation: Jeremiah doesn't make it into Herod's mouth. What Herod says to his servants is, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!" (Matthew 14:2). He names one man, and it's John. Herod says it plainly.

flags.problem: “Jeremiah doesn't make it into Herod's mouth” sounds awkward, and the final two sentences repeat that Herod named John.
flags.explanation: Jeremiah doesn't make it into Herod's mouth. What Herod says to his servants is, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!" (Matthew 14:2). He names one man, and it's John. Herod says it plainly.

flags.problem: “Wise is a nice word” is generic, and the explanation ends by repeating the quoted word without adding much.
flags.explanation: "Wise" is a nice word, but it's not John's word. Matthew records him saying, "It is not lawful for you to have her." (Matthew 14:4). This was about Herod and Herodias, his brother Philip's wife (Matthew 14:3). The word John used is lawful.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Right, friend. Mark says she heard about Jesus, "…and she came and fell at His feet." (Mark 7:25) Falling at someone's feet is a big, humble move. I think it shows how much her little girl mattered to her.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Yes, friend. Mark says the people "…begged Jesus to place His hand on him." (Mark 7:32) They brought a man who was deaf and hardly able to speak, and that was their ask. I think they cared about him a lot to bring him all that way to Jesus.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: Yes, friend. Mark says Jesus "…put His fingers into the man’s ears. Then He spit and touched the man’s tongue." (Mark 7:33) Those two places match the man's trouble, because he was deaf and hardly able to speak (Mark 7:32). Ears and tongue are your two answers.

flags.problem: It has 2 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
flags.explanation: That's the word, friend. Jesus says, “Ephphatha!” and Mark explains it means “Be opened!” (Mark 7:34) Then Mark says, "Immediately the man’s ears were opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak plainly." (Mark 7:35) I think that was quite a moment for him.

flags.problem: The joke doesn't click: a flour-covered apron doesn't explain how anyone discovered the hidden cookie box.
flags.explanation: That's right, friend. Mark says Jesus entered the house not wanting anyone to know He was there, but He "…was unable to escape their notice." (Mark 7:24) So the visit didn't stay a secret. I can't keep a secret in my own bakery either. I tried hiding a cookie box once, and my apron covered in flour gave me away.

flags.problem: Saying they brought the man 'all that way' suggests a distance the text doesn't give.
flags.explanation: Yes, friend. Mark says the people "…begged Jesus to place His hand on him." (Mark 7:32) They brought a man who was deaf and hardly able to speak, and that was their ask. I think they cared about him a lot to bring him all that way to Jesus.

flags.problem: Mark says they proclaimed it more widely, but 'Mark says the opposite' implies the text rules out their keeping quiet for a while. It doesn't specify that.
flags.answerText: They keep it to themselves for a while
flags.explanation: Mark says the opposite, friend. "But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it." (Mark 7:36) He doesn't say they held back at any point. He says they proclaimed it more widely.

flags.problem: The explanation repeats the same point in three ways without Papa Dorin's personality, even though the moment has room for a gentle laugh.
flags.answerText: They tell only their own families
flags.explanation: That's smaller than what Mark says, friend. "But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it." (Mark 7:36) Mark says they proclaimed it more widely, and he doesn't limit it to families. Telling only family is a much narrower thing than widely.

flags.problem: The timer laughing has no clear connection to planning a week's batches, so the joke fails the logic test.
flags.explanation: A week sounds nice and tidy, friend, but Luke 11:3 says, "Give us each day our daily bread." The word is day, not week. Picture me planning a whole week of cookie batches in one go, with the timer laughing at me. The prayer keeps it day-sized.

flags.problem: Counting boxes in his head does not explain why his mustache tangles, so the joke fails the logic test.
flags.explanation: A year in one ask? That's a big order, baker. The prayer in Luke 11:3 says, "Give us each day our daily bread." It's a day-sized request. I tried counting a year of cookie boxes in my head once, and my mustache got tangled.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through Jesus' sentence but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: That's the word, baker. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you." (Luke 11:9). Ask, seek, knock, and the last one comes with a door. Easy to remember, even for a stamper.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through Jesus' sentence but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Tapping on a window would get some strange looks, friend. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you." (Luke 11:9). The word is door, not window. I'd stick to doors.

flags.problem: The quotation starts partway through Jesus' sentence but has no opening ellipsis.
flags.explanation: That one sounds big and holy, baker, but it isn't the word here. Jesus says, "knock, and the door will be opened to you." (Luke 11:9). The word is door. Heavens isn't in that line.

flags.problem: For a false answer, the explanation must say what the text means. It says only that Jesus never says fathers do this, rather than explaining that His questions expect fathers not to give harmful things.
flags.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus asks, "What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?" (Luke 11:11-12). He asks these as questions about what a father would do, and He never says fathers do it. That's a lot of animals for two questions.

flags.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
flags.explanation: False, friend. Jesus says those who came before Him were thieves and robbers, and then adds that the sheep did not listen to them (John 10:8). It's the same kind of moment as the stranger's voice back in John 10:5. Tough crowd, those sheep.

flags.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
flags.explanation: Jesus says He has other sheep that are not of this fold, and He must bring them in as well. When He does, He says there will be "…one flock and one shepherd." (John 10:16). That's the picture, friend. One flock, and one shepherd leading it.

flags.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
flags.explanation: That's right. Jesus says, "No one takes it from Me…" (John 10:18). He lays it down of His own accord. He also says He has authority both to lay it down and to take it up again, a charge He received from His Father.

flags.problem: The joke compares climbing into a sheepfold another way with accidentally walking past a front door. The actions do not match.
flags.explanation: Jesus says whoever "…does not enter the sheepfold by the gate, but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber." (John 10:1). The gate is right there, and this guy skips it. I'd have to be one confused stamper to walk past my own front door.

flags.problem: The cookie-line joke is unclear: cookies and crumbs do not make a recognizable comparison for a shepherd leading sheep.
flags.explanation: That's backwards from what Jesus says. The shepherd "…goes on ahead of them, and his sheep follow him…" (John 10:4). The sheep are the ones following, and he's the one in front. If I stood at the back of my own cookie line, I'd be leading nobody but the crumbs.

flags.problem: Saying the thieves and robbers 'had their say' adds that they spoke. Jesus says the sheep did not listen to them, but does not say they spoke.
flags.explanation: Jesus says the opposite. About all who came before Him, He says, "…the sheep did not listen to them." (John 10:8). Those thieves and robbers had their say, and the sheep didn't listen. Not a single one of them got through to the flock.

flags.problem: The explanation has only two sentences. The opening fragment does not count toward the requested three to five sentences.
flags.explanation: No gate-building here. Jesus has already said He is the gate (John 10:9). About the shepherd, He says, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep." (John 10:11).

flags.problem: The statement that the sheep are not the hired hand's own comes from John 10:12, but only verses 13 and 11 are referenced.
flags.explanation: Jesus says, "The man runs away because he is a hired servant and is unconcerned for the sheep." (John 10:13). The sheep aren't his own, and the verse says he is unconcerned for them. That puts him in sharp contrast with the good shepherd, who lays down His life for the sheep (John 10:11).

flags.problem: Calling Jesus' authority 'a charge' blurs the distinction between His authority and the charge He says He received from His Father.
flags.explanation: That's right. Jesus says, "No one takes it from Me…" (John 10:18). He lays it down of His own accord. He also says He has authority both to lay it down and to take it up again, a charge He received from His Father.

flags.problem: “Close to a family question” is confusing because the selected answer is a family question.
flags.explanation: Close to a family question, but that's not what the commander asks. He says, "Do you speak Greek?" (Acts 21:37). Paul's father never comes up in this exchange. Language is the question on the table.

flags.problem: The cookie-crumble line and the closing sentence feel mild and generic for a moment with room for a stronger laugh.
flags.explanation: Right, baker. Paul motions to the crowd, and the text says, "A great hush came over the crowd…" (Acts 21:40). That's quiet enough to hear a cookie crumble. A hush like that is worth noticing.

flags.problem: “He wasn't told to sit in a seat” is an awkward, unclear contrast with being a witness.
flags.explanation: Judge sounds like a big job, so I see the pull. But Ananias says, "You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard." (Acts 22:15). He wasn't told to sit in a seat. He was told to tell.

flags.problem: “Just been led into Damascus blind” adds a sense of immediate timing the text doesn't give and skips over Paul's sight being restored before Ananias tells him to get up.
flags.answerText: Be baptized and wash his sins away
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. Ananias says, "And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name." (Acts 22:16). Paul had just been led into Damascus blind (Acts 22:11), and now he's being told to get up. It sounds to me like a friend who has no time to waste.

flags.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
flags.answerText: It is swallowed up in victory
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says a saying that is written will come to pass: "Death has been swallowed up in victory." (1 Corinthians 15:54). Death is the one getting swallowed. Not the other way around, and I'd say that's a good thing to know.

flags.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
flags.answerText: It is cast out of the land
flags.explanation: No land in this one, friend. Paul says a saying that is written will come to pass: "Death has been swallowed up in victory." (1 Corinthians 15:54). Swallowed up is the picture the saying gives. Nobody gets sent anywhere in it.

flags.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
flags.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul says, "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law." (1 Corinthians 15:56). He names sin as the sting of death. Then he adds that the power of sin is the law, all in one verse.

flags.problem: The explanation repeats the list without adding much personality or explanation.
flags.explanation: Right, baker. Paul says, "Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another." (1 Corinthians 15:39). That's one list with four kinds in it. Each group keeps its own kind of flesh, so nobody in that lineup gets mixed up with the others.

flags.problem: The comparison about a bird and fish wearing the same thing is unclear and does not make the joke click.
flags.explanation: Paul sees it differently, friend. He says, "Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another." (1 Corinthians 15:39). That's four kinds, not one. A bird and a fish are not wearing the same thing.

flags.problem: The explanation is flat and mostly repeats the answer and verse.
flags.answerText: Men and animals share one kind
flags.explanation: Close, but Paul keeps them apart, friend. He says, "Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another." (1 Corinthians 15:39). Men get one kind and animals get another. Every group in his list has its own.

flags.problem: The quotation begins partway through verse 42 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says, "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:42). Perishable means it can wear out. Imperishable means it won't. Picture a cookie that never goes stale, and you're close to the idea.

flags.problem: The quotation begins partway through verse 42 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul says, "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:42). The body is not raised the same as it was sown. Something new has happened to it.

flags.problem: The quotation begins partway through verse 42 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Nothing in the verse says anything about being unseen, friend. Paul says, "What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:42). Imperishable is the word he picks. It's about a body that doesn't wear out.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of verse 43 without an ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory." (1 Corinthians 15:43). Dishonor on one side, glory on the other. Quite a swing, and he's not done, because the same verse goes on to say sown in weakness, raised in power.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of verse 43 without an ellipsis.
flags.explanation: I see why you'd go there, friend, since it sits near dishonor. But Paul says, "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory." (1 Corinthians 15:43). He's not stacking one low word on another. He's flipping it around.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of verse 43 without an ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Paul has a louder word than that, friend. He says, "It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory." (1 Corinthians 15:43). Glory is the opposite of dishonor. Silence never makes it into the verse.

flags.problem: The first quotation stops before the end of verse 44 without an ellipsis, and the second starts partway through the verse without one.
flags.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says, "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). Then he adds, "If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). He treats the second as just as real as the first.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of verse 44 without an ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Paul draws a line between the two, friend. He says, "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). Sown is natural. Raised is spiritual. Using the same word twice wouldn't make much of a contrast.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of verse 44 without an ellipsis. The statement that dust comes up later also needs its reference, 1 Corinthians 15:47.
flags.explanation: Dust comes up later in the passage, friend, but not here. Paul says, "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." (1 Corinthians 15:44). The raised body is a spiritual one. Hold onto that dust thought for a minute.

flags.problem: The quotation begins partway through verse 45 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "the last Adam a life-giving spirit." (1 Corinthians 15:45). The first man Adam became a living being. The last Adam gives life.

flags.problem: The reference to Adam being in Eden introduces a Bible fact without a reference.
flags.explanation: Eden is a fair guess, friend, since Adam is in the neighborhood. But Paul says, "The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven." (1 Corinthians 15:47). He names heaven for the second man. Eden isn't in this verse.

flags.problem: The quotation from verse 51 begins partway through the verse without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Careful, friend. Paul says, "…flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:50). He doesn't say it can, just as it is. Right after that, he says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51).

flags.problem: The quotation from verse 51 begins partway through the verse without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "…flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable." (1 Corinthians 15:50). The perishable can't inherit the imperishable. That's why the very next verse matters, where Paul says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51).

flags.problem: The quotation begins partway through verse 51 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51). Some sleep and some don't, but nobody is left out of the change. All of us means all of us.

flags.problem: The quotation beginning with “We” starts partway through verse 51 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: Not in this verse, friend. Paul says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51). The word he uses is changed. He opens it with "Listen, I tell you a mystery…" and then names the change.

flags.problem: The quotation beginning with “We” starts partway through verse 51 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.explanation: This mystery isn't a warning, friend. Paul says, "We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed…" (1 Corinthians 15:51). The word is changed. He opens with "Listen, I tell you a mystery…" and then tells them what's coming.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of verse 52 without an ellipsis.
flags.answerText: In the twinkling of an eye
flags.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says it happens "in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:52). That's the whole change, and he gives it no more time than an instant. I can't even find my oven mitts that quick.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of verse 52 without an ellipsis.
flags.answerText: At the turning of a year
flags.explanation: Way too slow, friend. Paul says "in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:52). A year would be a very long wait. Paul says instant.

flags.problem: The quotation stops before the end of verse 52 without an ellipsis.
flags.answerText: In the passing of a day
flags.explanation: Still too slow, friend. Paul says "in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:52). A day is a whole lot of waiting. Paul says an instant, and he means it.

flags.problem: The explanation says honor belongs to another verse, but verse 43 speaks of dishonor and glory, not honor.
flags.explanation: Honor is a good guess, friend, since Paul said dishonor back in verse 43. Here he says, "For the perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality." (1 Corinthians 15:53). Mortal pairs with immortality. Honor belongs to another verse.

flags.problem: The quotation begins partway through verse 58 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.answerText: Their labor in the Lord is not in vain
flags.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Paul says, "Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58). Not in vain means it counts. So keep those ovens warm.

flags.problem: The quotation begins partway through verse 58 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.answerText: Others will see their good work
flags.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason, friend. He says, "Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58). The reason he names is that the labor is not in vain.

flags.problem: The quotation begins partway through verse 58 without a leading ellipsis.
flags.answerText: Their reward will come in this life
flags.explanation: Paul doesn't say when anything comes, friend, and he doesn't give that reason. He says, "Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58). Not in vain is the reason he gives.

flags.problem: The cookie-stamp comparison is Papa Dorin's, but “That's the picture Paul has of them” attributes it to Paul. The verse gives no such picture.
flags.explanation: Perfect, baker. Paul says, "For now we can go on living, as long as you are standing firm in the Lord." (1 Thessalonians 3:8). Standing firm is like a stamp pressed straight down into the dough, with no wobble and no slide. That's the picture Paul has of them. Their steadiness in the Lord means the world to him.

flags.problem: The explanation is flat, and “A good teacher always has more to share” is generic rather than distinctive to Papa Dorin.
flags.answerText: Supply what is lacking in their faith
flags.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith." (1 Thessalonians 3:10). They want to fill in what's missing in the Thessalonians' faith. A good teacher always has more to share.

flags.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
flags.explanation: Tychicus is a good guess, friend, but it isn't the name in this verse. Peter writes, "Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly…" (1 Peter 5:12). Silvanus is the one Peter regards as a faithful brother. Peter also says he wrote to encourage them and to testify that this is the true grace of God.

flags.problem: Referring to the card's statement draws attention to the lesson interface rather than speaking naturally to the baker.
flags.explanation: Peter says the opposite, friend. He calls himself "…a witness of Christ’s sufferings…" (1 Peter 5:1). So the card's statement is true, and the verse says it plainly. He's writing to people in a hard season, and he points to what he witnessed. I think that gives his words real weight.

flags.problem: The statement that the elders were told to be examples needs a reference to 1 Peter 5:3.
flags.explanation: That's flipped, friend. Peter says, "Young men, in the same way, submit yourselves to your elders." (1 Peter 5:5). The word is submit, not lead. The elders were just told to be examples, and now the young men get their own instruction.

flags.problem: The explanation is flat and repetitive. It restates Silvanus's role without much of Papa Dorin's warmth or personality.
flags.explanation: Timothy is a good name, friend, but it isn't the one Peter gives here. He writes, "Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly…" (1 Peter 5:12). Silvanus is the man he calls a faithful brother. The letter was written through him.
